newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-Peters prepares NZ markets for lower surplus.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Peters prepares NZ markets for lower surplus.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters on Friday began preparing the financial sector for a worse-than-expected fiscal outlook in next week's budget and both bond and bill markets largely took it in their stride.
For the second day in a row, Peters signalled clearly that budget surpluses would be much lower than some private forecasts, due largely to a series of one-off items.
The government's March 4 budget policy statement forecast surpluses of NZ$3.3 billion in 1997/8, $2.6 billion in 1998/9 and $3.5 billion in 1999/00 (June years).
Since then, ANZ Bank economists have forecast a 1997/98 surplus of NZ$2.9 billion and Bankers Trust New Zealand said last week it expected a surplus of between $2.8-3.0 billion.
Political sources, meanwhile, have speculated the 1997/98 projected surplus may come in at just under NZ$2.0 billion.
"Peters is doing what everybody thought he was going to do ... softening us up for a bit of a hard impact when the budget gets delivered next week," WestpacTrust economist Joselyn Stroombergen said.
"We've always been much more pessimistic than the treasury and the government as far as the fiscal numbers have gone," she said.
The main "negative surprise" in Peters' Friday speech was a warning that the government funding programme would also rise above previous estimates of about NZ$1.0 billion.
But financial markets were still seeing the "s" word -- surplus -- Stroombergen said. "They are still seeing surpluses, and so as long as they see that, they will be happy."

She was wary of Peter's comment that the deterioration was partly cyclical and that it had no impact on the future outlook. "If the operating surplus was going to be chopped in half from what they were thinking, then that certainly does have implications for further on down for the medium term outlook," she said.
Doyle Paterson Brown (DPB) economist Stephen Toplis said it was now clear that the the government's surplus would be well below expectations.
Toplis said he had forecast a relatively modest surplus of NZ$1.6 billion, but not for the reasons outlined by Peters.

DPB had not taken into account the one-offs outlined by Peters, but had taken the view that revenues were getting hammered, particularly on the corporate taxation side, and that the situation would not improve next year.
Eve Hayden, head of fixed interest dealing at ANZ Bank, said there was an immediate uptick in yields, particularly in the long bonds, after Peters' speech in Auckland this afternoon.
"I guess at the end of the day they were up five or six points following that in long bond terms," Hayden said.
"We were saying the bond tender programme was going to be about a billion dollars. Whether it's one billion or one point five it doesn't mean a hell of a lot of bonds really," she said.
Garlick and Co economist Matthew Goodson, said the government saw its GST (value added tax) returns as a good barometer for growth.

"But they have fallen quite substantially in the last month or two, as I understand it. That could perhaps account for some of it." He said he would not estimate the size of the surplus because it was unclear how big some of the one-off items were.
